Concrete Driveways · St. Cloud, FL

Concrete Driveways for St. Cloud Homes

A new or replacement concrete driveway in St. Cloud costs $6–$15 per sq ft installed as of October 2026. The city's Building Division doesn't treat the driveway surface itself as a permit item, but Public Works still charges a $110 basic fee plus $30 for every curb cut where the new apron meets the street.

By the Opera Concrete & Pavers estimating team · Updated October 1, 2026

Public Works prices the apron by the piece

St. Cloud splits a driveway job into separate line items rather than one flat permit fee: a $110 basic fee applies per permit, a curb cut is $30, a driveway inspection runs $100, and a sidewalk inspection is $60 (City of St. Cloud, Public Works Fees). Those charges sit with Public Works, a different office than the Building Division that handles the “Residential Other” and pool-and-spa permits, so a quote that only budgets for one office's fees can come up short once the other one weighs in. City Hall is at 1300 9th St., 407-957-7300, the number to call before ordering concrete for a driveway that touches the right-of-way at all.

The Building Division's own list draws a line most homeowners don't expect

St. Cloud's permit page separates “No Permit Required” items from “Permit Required” ones, and a driveway reseal on an existing on-site surface falls on the easy side of that line, with a note that anything reaching into the right-of-way still needs Public Works and Engineering sign-off first (City of St. Cloud, Permit Information). A full tear-out and repour, by contrast, changes the footprint and the apron at the same time, the kind of scope that pulls in both offices rather than one. Confirming which category a specific job falls into before the first yard of concrete is ordered avoids a stop-work call mid-pour.

Ridge Sand Doesn't Behave Like Flatwoods Soil

The sand ridge soils west of Orlando, Candler, Astatula and Tavares, drain almost too well: the water table can sit more than 80 inches down. That sounds like easier ground to build on, but loose, excessively drained sand does not hold a compactor's pass the way a firmer soil does, and it can shift under the plate instead of locking together. On a ridge lot in St. Cloud, we wet the material enough to bind it, then compact in shallow lifts rather than one deep pass. Skip that step and the driveway can still settle later, just for the opposite reason a flatwoods lot would.

Demolition Day Looks Nothing Like Pour Day

Replacing an existing driveway starts with tearing out what is there, breaking up and hauling off the old slab before any new base work begins. That is a separate phase from forming, grading and pouring, and on a St. Cloud job it usually happens on its own day or two rather than the same day as the new pour. Once the old concrete is gone, we can finally see and test the subgrade underneath it, which sometimes changes the plan if the soil under a decades-old slab turns out wetter or weaker than expected. Skipping ahead to forming before demolition is fully cleared is how schedules slip.

A St. Cloud driveway replacement, worked out with both fees stacked

Say a 20 by 22 foot driveway, 440 square feet, gets torn out and repoured along with a new apron at the curb. At $6–$15 per sq ft installed, the slab itself runs roughly $2,640 to $6,600 before Public Works' fees are added. The apron work alone adds the $110 basic fee, the $30 curb cut and the $100 driveway inspection, about $240 total, on top of whatever the Building Division charges for the rest of the pour. Repouring only the section back from the street skips that $240, though the two sections of concrete then meet at a new joint instead of one continuous pour.

Timing the Saw Cut Changes What the Joint Looks Like

A control joint cut too late can miss the crack it was meant to control, and one cut too early can tear the surface instead of slicing it cleanly. Early-entry saws go in about 1 to 4 hours after finishing, while a conventional wet saw waits 4 to 12 hours until the concrete has firmed up enough to cut without ravelling the edge. The right window shifts with temperature and humidity on a given St. Cloud pour day, which is why we watch the slab rather than work off a fixed clock. Getting this step wrong shows up later as a ragged joint edge or a crack that wandered off the cut line.

Oversized Panels Crack Wherever They Want To

A driveway poured without enough control joints, or with panels larger than roughly 8 to 12 feet across on a standard 4-inch slab, does not crack less, it just cracks somewhere nobody chose. The same risk shows up when a layout wraps the concrete around a porch step or utility pad into an L shape instead of planning extra joints at that corner. A St. Cloud driveway with either problem usually looks fine for the first year, then develops a crack that runs diagonally across a panel instead of along a joint line, which is both a weaker crack and a worse-looking one than the joints were designed to produce.

Why the Groove in a Control Joint Needs to Stay Clear

The groove cut into a driveway's control joints has to reach at least a quarter of the slab's thickness to do its job of controlling where the concrete cracks, and that same depth is what lets sand, dirt and organic debris pack into the joint over time if nobody checks it. On a St. Cloud driveway, keeping those grooves swept out, especially heading into the rainy season, keeps them working the way they were cut to work instead of silting in and trapping water against the edges of each panel. It is a five-minute task with a broom, not a specialty job, and it is easy to let slide for years at a time.

Frequently asked questions

Does St. Cloud charge a flat fee for a driveway permit?

No. Public Works itemizes the charges instead: a $110 basic fee, $30 per curb cut, $100 for a driveway inspection and $60 for a sidewalk inspection. A job touching more than one of those categories pays more than one line item.

Is a concrete driveway on the city's no-permit list?

A reseal of an existing on-site surface is. A full replacement that changes the apron at the street is different, since that work reaches into the right-of-way and needs Public Works and Engineering approval before it starts.

Which office do I call first for a St. Cloud driveway job?

Public Works and Engineering, reachable through City Hall at 407-957-7300, is the office that reviews anything touching the curb or the right-of-way. The Building Division handles the separate permit list for pads, walls and pools.
